stem: Match each learning type to its goal (Lecture 9).
solutionSteps: Supervised → learn a function mapping x → y
Unsupervised → learn the hidden structure of unlabelled data
Generative modelling → learn a model whose samples look like the training distribution
takeaway: Generative: P_model ≈ P_data.
source: Lecture 9, slide 2-4
right: learn the hidden structure of unlabelled data
learn a function mapping x → y
learn a model whose samples look like the training distribution

stem: Why are generative models useful (Lecture 9)? (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: Three motivations.
source: Lecture 9, slide 5-7
options: Debiasing datasets by uncovering underlying features

stem: In the shadow example, what are the latent variables?
takeaway: Hidden factors = z; observed result = x.
source: Lecture 9, slide 8
options: Object shape, orientation, light direction and light distance

stem: Density estimation and sample generation are the two goals of generative modelling in Lecture 9.
takeaway: Learn P_model(x) similar to P_data(x).
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: What is the autoencoder's training loss?
takeaway: Input = target.
source: Lecture 9, slide 14
options: ‖x − x̂‖², comparing the input with its reconstruction

stem: A smaller latent space (e.g. 2D instead of 5D) gives a tighter bottleneck and usually blurrier reconstructions.
takeaway: Bottleneck size trades compression vs quality.
source: Lecture 9, slide 15

stem: In a denoising autoencoder, the reconstruction is compared with…
takeaway: Noisy in, clean target.
source: Lecture 9, slide 16

whyWrong.C: That would learn to reproduce noise.

stem: Select ALL applications/limitations of standard autoencoders (Lecture 9). (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: AEs aren't good generators.
source: Lecture 9, slide 17
options: Excellent generation from randomly sampled codes
Anomaly detection via high reconstruction error

stem: What is the key difference between a VAE and a traditional autoencoder?
takeaway: Probabilistic twist.
source: Lecture 9, slide 20-21
options: The encoder outputs a mean μ and standard deviation σ, and z is sampled from them

stem: KL term for one latent dimension with μ = 0.5, σ = 1: ½(μ² + σ² − 1 − ln σ²) = ______.
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: Regularising with the normal prior encourages means toward 0 and variances toward 1, which gives continuity and completeness.
takeaway: Close points decode similarly; samples decode meaningfully.
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: Why is the reparameterisation trick needed?
takeaway: z = μ + σ⊙ε moves randomness to ε.
source: Lecture 9, slide 31-34
options: Gradients cannot be backpropagated through a random sampling node
To speed up the forward pass

stem: In a β-VAE with β > 1, what happens?
takeaway: β = 250: head rotation without smile change.
source: Lecture 9, slide 36
options: The latent bottleneck is constrained more, encouraging disentangled factors

stem: Match each VAE loss term to its role.
solutionSteps: Reconstruction loss → make x̂ close to x (e.g. ‖x − x̂‖²)
KL regulariser → keep q(z|x) close to the prior N(0, I)
takeaway: Two terms.
source: Lecture 9, slide 22-27
right: keep q(z|x) close to the prior N(0, I)
make x̂ close to x (e.g. ‖x − x̂‖²)

stem: In a GAN, what does the discriminator learn?
takeaway: D outputs a realness score.
source: Lecture 9, slide 40
options: To distinguish real training samples from generated samples
To encode images into μ and σ
To generate new samples from noise

stem: At the ideal GAN equilibrium, the discriminator outputs D(x) ≈ 0.5 because generated and real distributions match.
takeaway: Neither source is more likely.
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: The generator learns one output that fools D very well and ignores the other modes of the data. This is…
takeaway: Matches one region, misses diversity.
source: Lecture 9, slide 46

stem: Select ALL true statements about GAN training (Lecture 9). (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: Adversarial min-max.
source: Lecture 9, slide 44-51
options: D maximises E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 − D(G(z)))]
Training alternates between D and G
After training, the generator alone creates new data
G minimises the same expression; the real term is constant w.r.t. G
G is trained on real images directly

source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: How does an autoregressive model generate a sentence?
takeaway: Predict, sample, append, repeat.
source: Lecture 9, slide 58
options: Predict a distribution for the next token, sample it, append it, repeat
Decode a single latent vector in one step

stem: With causal masking, autoregressive models generate all tokens of a new sentence in one parallel step.
solutionSteps: TRAINING is parallel across positions; GENERATION is sequential, token by token.
takeaway: Mask = no peeking at the future.
source: Lecture 9, slide 60
why: TRAINING is parallel across positions; GENERATION is sequential, token by token.

stem: Match each domain to its autoregressive model (Lecture 9 table).
takeaway: Same idea, different elements.
source: Lecture 9, slide 62

stem: In FVSBN, which inputs does the output unit x̂₄ receive?
takeaway: x̂₄ = σ(b₄ + w₄₁x₁ + w₄₂x₂ + w₄₃x₃).
source: Lecture 9, slide 59
options: Only the earlier visible variables x₁, x₂, x₃

stem: FVSBN: b₄ = −1, w₄₁ = 2, w₄₂ = 0.5, w₄₃ = −1, x = (1, 0, 1). The input to the sigmoid is ______.
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: What does the diffusion denoising network ε_θ(xₜ, t) learn to predict during training?
takeaway: MSE loss ‖ε̂ − ε‖².
source: Lecture 9, slide 65
options: The noise ε that was added to produce xₜ
Whether xₜ is real or fake

stem: In the forward process, as t approaches T, xₜ approaches pure Gaussian noise N(0, I).
takeaway: Clear image → nearly pure noise.
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: Select ALL true statements about text-guided latent diffusion. (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: Prompt steers the denoising.
source: Lecture 9, slide 68
options: It decodes to an image once at the end
It needs no noise at all
A text encoder conditions each denoising step
It denoises in a compact latent space

whyWrong.B: Incorrect: Starts from random latent noise.

stem: Lecture 9 'Four ways to generate new data': match each model to its process.
solutionSteps: Autoregressive → earlier elements → next element → repeat
Diffusion → Gaussian noise → denoise → repeat → image
takeaway: Slide 70.
source: Lecture 9, slide 70

stem: In ControlNet (Lecture 9), what does the pose map control?
takeaway: Same spatial guide, varied prompts.
source: Lecture 9, slide 69
options: Where things appear (spatial structure), while text describes the content

source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: Generative modelling aims to learn P_model(x) similar to P_______(x).
takeaway: Lecture 9 slide 4.
source: Lecture 9 (Generative AI)

stem: A VAE encoder outputs μ = [0, -0.8] and σ = [1, 0.8]. Compute D_KL(q(z|x) ‖ N(0, I)) = ½ Σⱼ (μⱼ² + σⱼ² − 1 − log σⱼ²) using natural logs.
takeaway: KL is 0 only when μ = 0 and σ = 1: it pulls encodings toward the standard normal prior.
